unit.unitOverview: Disagreeing in a second language is where fluent people most often sound rude by accident, and the reason is almost never grammar. This unit separates fact from opinion, gives you the frames English uses to mark a view as a view, and covers the concession move that makes a disagreement sound considered. It ends with the same disagreement written twice, because the difference between the two is entirely in the framing.
unit.learningPath:

visual.lectureScript:
This unit is about the thing that most often goes wrong for people whose English is otherwise good. You disagree with somebody and it lands badly, and you cannot work out why, because every word was correct.
The reason is almost never grammar. It is framing.
First pattern: fact and opinion, and telling them apart.
A fact can be checked. The report is forty pages. The delivery arrived on Tuesday. Costs rose by twelve per cent.
An opinion cannot. The report is too long. The delivery was late. The increase was unreasonable.
Notice how close those pairs are. Forty pages is a fact; too long is a judgement about that fact. Arrived on Tuesday is a fact; was late is a judgement, and it depends on when it was due.
The test is simple: could two honest, well-informed people disagree about it? If yes, it is an opinion.
And here is why it matters more than it sounds. In English, stating an opinion as though it were a fact is the commonest cause of a conversation going wrong. This report is too long is a statement about the world. I think this report is too long is a statement about me. The second invites a reply; the first invites a fight.
So the practical rule is: mark your opinions as opinions. It costs two words and it changes the temperature of the whole exchange.
Second pattern: the frames that do the marking.
There is a range, and it runs from tentative to firm.
At the tentative end: I tend to think, it seems to me, I would have thought, my impression is.
In the middle: I think, in my view, as far as I can see, personally.
At the firm end: I am convinced, I have no doubt, I am certain.
All of them mark a view as a view. What differs is how much weight you are putting behind it, and choosing the wrong strength is a real error.
Using a firm frame for a small point sounds heavy. I am convinced we should order more envelopes is comic.
Using a tentative frame for something you are sure of sounds weak, and worse, it invites people to talk you out of a position you actually hold.
There is one more frame worth having, and it is the most useful in the list. As I understand it. That marks your statement as based on information which might be incomplete, and it is how you can be firm about a fact and still leave room to be wrong. As I understand it, the deadline is the fourteenth. If you are wrong, nothing collapses.
Third pattern: agreeing and disagreeing.
Agreeing is easy in any language, so I will spend one sentence on it: agree fully with I agree or exactly, agree partly with I agree up to a point or that is true, but.
Disagreeing is the difficult one, and English has a strong preference about how it is done.
The preference is: concede first, then disagree.
That is true, but I think the timing is the problem.
I take your point. However, the cost has changed since then.
I agree with most of that. My only reservation is the deadline.
Every one of those begins by giving something away, and then disagrees. The concession is not politeness for its own sake — it does real work. It tells the other person you have understood them, which means your disagreement is about the substance rather than about not having listened.
The version without a concession is much harder to hear. No, the timing is the problem. That is grammatically fine and it starts an argument rather than a discussion.
And there is a useful softener: my only reservation is. It signals that you accept the rest, which is usually true and rarely said.
Fourth pattern, and this is not grammar at all.
Tone in English is carried by things learners are rarely taught, and three of them do most of the work.
Directness. English disagreement is usually indirect, and the indirectness is expected rather than evasive. I am not sure that would work is a full disagreement. Somebody hearing it knows you disagree.
Hedging. Might, perhaps, tend to, fairly, somewhat, a bit. These are not weakness. In a disagreement they signal that you are leaving room, and their absence reads as certainty even when you did not intend it.
And the word just. It makes a statement smaller. I just think the timing is wrong is softer than I think the timing is wrong, and both are softer than the timing is wrong.
Here is the thing that catches people. The strength of your English does not translate to the strength of your opinion. A learner using simple, direct sentences can sound far more forceful than they mean, purely because the hedges are missing. That is not a reflection of what you think; it is a mechanical result of vocabulary.
So if you have ever been surprised by somebody's reaction to something you said, this is the most likely cause, and it is fixable with about six words.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: Could Two Honest People Disagree?
readings.passageScript:
The report is forty pages.
The report is too long.
One of those can be checked and one cannot, and the distinction decides how the sentence will be received.
The test is a single question: could two honest, well-informed people disagree about it?
Nobody can honestly disagree about forty pages. Two people can easily disagree about too long, because too long depends on what the report is for, who is reading it and how much time they have.
Some pairs are much closer than they look.
The delivery arrived on Tuesday. Fact.
The delivery was late. Opinion — it depends on when it was due, and whether the delay was agreed.
Costs rose by twelve per cent. Fact.
The increase was unreasonable. Opinion, entirely.
She did not reply. Fact.
She ignored me. Opinion, and a significant one, because it attributes an intention that the fact does not contain.
That last pair is worth sitting with. She did not reply is checkable. She ignored me adds a decision on her part, which is exactly the thing you cannot see.
Here is why this matters more than it sounds.
Stating an opinion as though it were a fact is the commonest cause of a conversation going wrong in English, and it is almost never intentional.
This report is too long is a statement about the world. If somebody disagrees, they have to contradict you.
I think this report is too long is a statement about you. If somebody disagrees, they only have to have a different view.
The second invites a reply. The first invites a fight.
Two words, and they change what kind of exchange follows. That is the highest return on effort in this unit.

readings.title: Why Simple English Sounds Blunt
readings.passageScript:
Here is something that catches almost everybody, and it is not a failure of grammar.
The strength of your English does not translate to the strength of your opinion.
A learner with a working vocabulary produces short, direct sentences. The timing is wrong. That will not work. I disagree.
Every one of those is correct. Every one of them is also considerably more forceful than the speaker usually intends, and the reason is mechanical: the hedges are missing.
English carries a great deal of tone in small words that are easy to leave out because they add no information.
Might, perhaps, tend to, fairly, somewhat, a bit, rather, quite.
I am not sure that would work is a full disagreement. Anybody hearing it knows you disagree. It is not evasive and it is not weak — it is the normal register for disagreement between people who are not in conflict.
The timing might be a problem says the same thing as the timing is wrong, and the difference in how it lands is very large.
Then there is just, which makes a statement smaller.
The timing is wrong.
I think the timing is wrong.
I just think the timing is wrong.
Those three are in increasing order of softness, and the last one is what most first-language speakers would say in an ordinary work disagreement.
The practical consequence is this. If you have ever said something reasonable and been surprised by the reaction, the most likely cause is not what you said but how little padding it had. It is not a reflection of what you think. It is a mechanical result of using the words you have.
And the fix is small. Six or seven hedging words, deployed deliberately, will bring how you sound into line with what you mean.
One caution in the other direction. Hedging everything has its own cost. Somebody who says perhaps and I might be wrong before every sentence is difficult to read, and people stop knowing when they hold a position. Hedge the disagreements; state the facts plainly.

readings.title: The Same Objection, Twice
readings.setting: A reply to a colleague's proposal, drafted twice by the same person.
readings.passageScript:
VERSION A - sent at 17:40

  I don't agree with this. The timing is
  wrong. We can't do a system change in
  December, that's our busiest month. The
  costs are also wrong - you've used last
  year's figures. And nobody has asked the
  warehouse team what they think.

  We should wait until spring.

-----------------------------------------

  VERSION B - what was sent the next
  morning instead

  Thanks for putting this together - the
  case for replacing the system is strong
  and I don't think anyone disputes that
  it needs doing.

  My reservation is about timing rather
  than the plan itself. December is our
  busiest month, and I suspect a system
  change then would cost us more in
  disruption than we'd save in the first
  year.

  One factual point: I think the costs on
  page 3 may be last year's figures - the
  supplier raised prices in March. Worth
  checking.

  I'd also want to hear from the warehouse
  team before we commit, mainly because
  they'll carry most of the change.

  Would a spring start be workable?

     yes -> OPINION
     no  -> FACT

PAIRS THAT LOOK ALIKE
  The report is forty pages.   FACT
  The report is too long.      OPINION

  It arrived on Tuesday.       FACT
  It was late.                 OPINION

  Costs rose by 12 per cent.   FACT
  The increase was unreasonable. OPINION

  She did not reply.           FACT
  She ignored me.              OPINION
  ^ adds an intention you cannot see.

WHY IT MATTERS
  "This report is too long."
     a statement about THE WORLD.
     To disagree, they must contradict you.

  "I think this report is too long."
     a statement about YOU.
     To disagree, they need a different view.

  The first invites a fight.
  The second invites a reply.

  Two words. Mark your opinions.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say a delivery came later than it should have.
1. Apply the test to it was late. Could two honest people disagree? Yes — it depends when it was due and whether a delay was agreed.
2. So it is an opinion, and stating it flat will read as an accusation.
3. Separate the fact from the judgement. The fact is: it arrived on Tuesday.
4. Mark the judgement: I think that is later than we agreed.
5. Result: It arrived on Tuesday, which I think is later than we agreed.
Now the reader can check the fact and consider the judgement separately, and if they think Tuesday was correct they can say so without contradicting you about anything.
Compare the unmarked version: the delivery was late. That is one sentence which mixes a fact and a judgement, and anybody who disagrees has to take issue with the whole thing.
grammar.commonMistake: Stating a judgement in the grammar of a fact — the report is too long, she ignored me, the costs are wrong. Each of those is a view wearing the clothes of an observation, and the listener has no way to disagree without contradicting you. The other error is the opposite: marking a genuine fact with I think, which makes checkable information sound uncertain.
grammar.memoryTip: Could two honest people disagree? Then say I think.
grammar.practice:
Write FACT or OPINION. For each opinion, rewrite it with a frame.
1. The report is forty pages.
2. The report is too long.
3. The delivery arrived on Tuesday.
4. The delivery was late.
5. Costs rose by twelve per cent.
6. The increase was unreasonable.
7. She did not reply.
8. She ignored me.
grammar.answerKey:
1. FACT  2. OPINION — I think the report is too long.
3. FACT  4. OPINION — I think the delivery was later than agreed.
5. FACT  6. OPINION — I think the increase was unreasonable.
7. FACT  8. OPINION — I got the impression she was ignoring me.
Numbers 7 and 8 are the closest pair. Did not reply is checkable; ignored adds a decision on her part that nothing in the fact establishes.
Notice that in 4 the rewrite also made the judgement more specific — later than agreed rather than simply late — which gives the other person something concrete to respond to.

grammar.title: Opinion frames, from tentative to firm
grammar.explanation: All of these mark a view as a view. What differs is how much weight you put behind it, and choosing the wrong strength is a real error in both directions.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
TENTATIVE
  I tend to think...
  It seems to me...
  I would have thought...
  My impression is...
  I suspect...

MIDDLE
  I think...
  In my view...
  As far as I can see...
  Personally, ...

FIRM
  I am convinced...
  I have no doubt...
  I am certain...

CHOOSING WRONG, BOTH WAYS
  firm frame, small point
     "I am convinced we should order
      more envelopes."   -> comic
  tentative frame, held position
     invites people to talk you out of
     something you actually believe.

THE MOST USEFUL ONE
  As I understand it, ...
  ^ marks it as based on information that
    might be incomplete. Lets you be firm
    about a fact and still be wrong safely.

     "As I understand it, the deadline
      is the fourteenth."
grammar.workedExample:
You are fairly sure the deadline has moved, but you have not checked.
1. Is this a fact or an opinion? A fact — the deadline either moved or it did not.
2. But your information might be wrong, and that is a different thing from having a view.
3. So use the information frame, not an opinion frame: As I understand it, the deadline has moved to the fourteenth.
4. If you are wrong, nothing collapses. You reported your understanding accurately.
Now a genuine opinion you hold firmly. You believe the December timing will fail.
1. It is an opinion — honest people could disagree.
2. How strongly do you hold it? Firmly.
3. But a firm frame in a first message is heavy. The middle is usually right to open with: I think a December change would cost us more than it saves.
4. Keep I am convinced for the second exchange, if you are still holding the position after hearing the reply.
Starting firm leaves you nowhere to go.
grammar.commonMistake: Using I am convinced or I have no doubt for ordinary points, which sounds disproportionate and makes later firmness meaningless. The opposite error is hedging a position you actually hold — I suppose maybe it might not work invites the other person to argue you out of something you believe, and then you have to fight back from a weaker place than you started.
grammar.memoryTip: Open in the middle. Keep the firm frames for the second exchange.
grammar.practice:
Choose a frame of the right strength and write the sentence.
1. You are fairly sure the deadline moved. You have not checked.
2. You firmly believe a December change will fail.
3. You have a mild preference for the second option.
4. You are certain the figures on page 3 are last year's.
5. You suspect the problem is elsewhere but have no evidence.
6. You have a general impression that morale has dropped.
grammar.answerKey:
1. As I understand it, the deadline has moved. — an information frame, not an opinion frame
2. I think a December change would cost more than it saves. — the middle; keep I am convinced in reserve
3. I would probably go for the second option. — tentative, matching a mild preference
4. The figures on page 3 are last year's. — a checkable fact, so no frame at all
5. I suspect the problem is elsewhere. — tentative, and honest about the lack of evidence
6. My impression is that morale has dropped. — tentative, and impression is exactly the right word
Number 4 is the one worth checking. It is a fact you are certain of, so adding I think would make checkable information sound uncertain. Frames are for opinions and for uncertain information, not for things you know.
Number 2 opens in the middle deliberately. Firm frames in a first message leave you nowhere to escalate to.

grammar.title: Agreeing and disagreeing
grammar.explanation: Agreeing is easy in any language. Disagreeing is where English has a strong preference, and the preference is: concede first, then disagree.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
AGREEING
  fully:   I agree. / Exactly. / Quite.
  partly:  I agree up to a point.
           That is true, but...
           I share your concern about X.

DISAGREEING - CONCEDE FIRST
  That is true, but I think the timing
     is the problem.
  I take your point. However, the cost
     has changed since then.
  I agree with most of that. My only
     reservation is the deadline.
  I accept the principle. I am less sure
     about the timing.

WHY THE CONCESSION IS NOT DECORATION
  it tells them you UNDERSTOOD them,
  so your disagreement is about the
  substance, not about not listening.

  Without it: "No, the timing is the
  problem." -> an argument, not a
  discussion.

THE MOST USEFUL SOFTENER
  My only reservation is...
  ^ signals you accept everything else,
    which is usually true and rarely said.

NARROW THE TARGET
  "I don't dispute the figures, only
   what they mean."
grammar.workedExample:
A colleague proposes a system change in December. You think the plan is right and the timing is wrong.
1. Find what you genuinely agree with. The plan itself — the system does need replacing.
2. Concede that first, and be specific rather than formulaic: The case for replacing it is strong and I do not think anyone disputes that.
3. Now narrow the target so they know what is actually under attack: My reservation is about timing rather than the plan itself.
4. Then disagree, with a reason: December is our busiest month, and I suspect a change then would cost more in disruption than it saves.
Notice what step 3 achieves. Without it, they have to defend the whole proposal. With it, they only have to think about December.
Compare the version with no concession: I do not agree with this. The timing is wrong. Same objection, and now the other person is defending everything.
grammar.commonMistake: Disagreeing without conceding anything, which is grammatically fine and reads as a rejection of the whole. The other error is a formulaic concession — I take your point, but used as a ritual rather than meant. If the concession names nothing specific, the listener hears it as a throat-clearing noise before the disagreement, and it does no work.
grammar.memoryTip: Concede something real, narrow the target, then disagree.
grammar.practice:
Write a disagreement for each, conceding first and narrowing the target.
1. A proposal is good but the timing is wrong.
2. The figures are right but the conclusion drawn from them is not.
3. The plan is sound but nobody has asked the people who will do the work.
4. You accept the principle and doubt it can be done in the budget.
5. You agree with everything except one deadline.
6. Somebody says a delivery was late. You think it arrived when agreed.
grammar.answerKey:
Model answers — yours will differ.
1. The case for it is strong. My reservation is about timing rather than the plan itself.
2. I do not dispute the figures, only what they are being taken to show.
3. I think the plan is sound. I would want to hear from the team who will carry it before we commit.
4. I accept the principle entirely. I am much less sure it can be done for that money.
5. I agree with almost all of this. My only reservation is the deadline.
6. I think it arrived on the day we agreed — as I understand it, the date was the fourteenth. Am I wrong about that?
Every one concedes something specific before disagreeing, and every one names exactly what is under attack.
Number 6 combines this card with card 1: it separates the fact from the judgement, uses an information frame, and ends with a question rather than a verdict.

grammar.title: Tone: hedging and directness
grammar.explanation: Not grammar. English carries tone in small words that add no information and are therefore easy to leave out — and leaving them out makes you sound stronger than you mean.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE HEDGES
  might, perhaps, tend to, fairly,
  somewhat, a bit, rather, quite,
  I suspect, I imagine, probably

THE SCALE - same content, three strengths
  The timing is wrong.
  I think the timing is wrong.
  I just think the timing is wrong.

JUST MAKES IT SMALLER
  "I just wanted to check..."
  "I'd just add one thing."

INDIRECTNESS IS EXPECTED, NOT EVASIVE
  "I'm not sure that would work."
  ^ a FULL disagreement. They know.

THE MECHANICAL PROBLEM
  Simple English -> short direct sentences
  -> hedges missing -> sounds forceful.

  It is NOT what you think.
  It is the words you have.

THE CAUTION
  Hedge everything and people stop knowing
  when you hold a position.
     hedge the DISAGREEMENTS
     state the FACTS plainly
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say a plan will not work.
1. The bare version: That will not work.
2. Ask what it sounds like. It is a verdict, delivered flat, with no room for the other person to be right.
3. Add an opinion frame: I do not think that will work.
4. Add a hedge: I am not sure that would work.
5. Notice the tense shift — would rather than will. The conditional is itself a hedge, and it is why the second conditional felt polite in Unit 5.
Result: I am not sure that would work. Anybody hearing this knows you disagree, and nobody has been backed into a corner.
Now the opposite direction. You are reporting a fact.
1. The figures on page 3 are last year's.
2. Do not hedge this. It is checkable, and hedging it makes real information sound like an impression.
Hedge the disagreement. State the fact.
grammar.commonMistake: Producing bare, direct sentences and being surprised at the reaction. This is not rudeness and it is not a grammar error — it is the mechanical result of a working vocabulary that has not yet picked up the padding. The opposite error is hedging everything, including facts, which makes it impossible for anyone to tell what you actually think.
grammar.memoryTip: Hedge the disagreements. State the facts plainly.
grammar.practice:
Soften each disagreement without weakening the point. Then say which one should not be softened.
1. That will not work.
2. The timing is wrong.
3. You have used the wrong figures.
4. Nobody asked the warehouse team.
5. This is too expensive.
6. The figures on page 3 are from last year.
grammar.answerKey:
1. I am not sure that would work.
2. I think the timing might be a problem.
3. I think the costs on page 3 may be last year's figures — worth checking.
4. I would want to hear from the warehouse team before we commit.
5. I suspect this may be more expensive than it looks.
6. Should not be softened. It is a checkable fact, and hedging it would make real information sound like an impression.
Numbers 3 and 6 are the same subject and they are handled differently on purpose. Number 3 is an accusation about somebody's work and takes a hedge. Number 6 is a plain statement of what the figures are and does not.
Notice that number 1 shifted from will to would. The conditional is itself a hedge, which is the same mechanism that makes if I were you polite in Unit 5.

writing.title: Writing 1 — A disagreement, twice
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Choose something you genuinely disagree with — a decision, a proposal, a policy, an argument you have read.
Write your objection twice.
Version A: bare. No frames, no hedges, no concession. Six to eight sentences.
Version B: your real version. Open with a specific concession, narrow the target, mark every opinion, hedge the disagreements but not the facts, and end with a question.
Then write three lines: what B concedes, what it narrows the disagreement to, and which sentence in B is a plain fact you deliberately did not hedge.
writing.modelText:
Version B only, since A is an exercise in doing it badly:
Thanks for pulling this together — I think the case for moving the rota to a four-week cycle is strong, and the staffing maths clearly works better than what we have now.
My reservation is about how it is introduced rather than the cycle itself. Under the current proposal everybody changes in the same week, and I suspect that would leave us with nobody who knows the old pattern if something goes wrong in the first fortnight.
One factual point: the proposal says the current cycle is three weeks. It has been two weeks since March. That changes the transition arithmetic on page 2.
I would also want to hear from the weekend team before we commit, mainly because the change affects them more than anybody.
Would a staggered introduction over three weeks be workable?

1. B concedes that the four-week cycle is right and that the staffing maths is better.
2. It narrows the disagreement to the method of introduction, not the cycle.
3. The unhedged fact is that the current cycle has been two weeks since March — that is checkable, and hedging it would make real information sound like an impression.
writing.successCriteria: Both versions make the same objections; version B opens with a specific concession, narrows the target explicitly, marks every opinion with a frame, hedges disagreements but leaves facts plain, and ends with a question; three lines of commentary identifying the concession, the narrowing and the unhedged fact
writing.support: Write B first. Writing A afterwards is easier than writing badly from a blank page, and stripping B shows you exactly which words were doing the softening.
writing.extension: Give B to somebody and ask them what you were objecting to. If they name the whole proposal rather than the one part, the narrowing did not work.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Sixteen statements sorted
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write sixteen statements about something you know well — a workplace, a process, a place, an organisation.
Eight must be facts and eight must be opinions, mixed in any order.
Label each one.

1. The warehouse has 340 pallet spaces. FACT
2. The warehouse is too small. OPINION — I think it is too small for the volume we now handle. (middle: a considered view)
3. Deliveries arrive between 06:00 and 08:00. FACT
4. The delivery window is too tight. OPINION — I suspect the window is too tight for three drivers. (tentative: I have not measured it)
5. Two staff left in the last quarter. FACT
6. Morale has dropped. OPINION — My impression is that morale has dropped. (tentative: impression is the right word)
7. The forklift was serviced in March. FACT
8. The forklift is unreliable. OPINION — I am convinced the forklift is unreliable. (firm: it has failed four times)
9. There is one working printer. FACT
10. Nobody has asked the night shift. FACT
11. The night shift should have been consulted. OPINION — In my view the night shift should have been consulted. (middle)
12. The rota changed in March. FACT
13. The new rota is worse. OPINION — I tend to think the new rota is worse. (tentative: others disagree)
14. Three of the racking bays are unlabelled. FACT
15. The labelling is a safety issue. OPINION — I have no doubt the labelling is a safety issue. (firm: it is a hazard)
16. The site is 4km from the depot. FACT

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the two versions
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Use the two versions in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. What three objections do both versions make?
2. What does B's opening sentence achieve that A's does not?
3. A says the costs are wrong. B says they may be last year's figures. Which is more useful, and why?
4. What does B's closing question do that A's closing sentence does not?
5. B is longer than A and makes no additional objections. What is the extra length doing?
writing.modelText:
1. That December is the wrong month for a system change, that the costs use last year's figures, and that the warehouse team has not been consulted.
2. It concedes something specific and true — the case for replacing the system is strong and nobody disputes it needs doing. That tells the reader the proposal itself is not under attack, so they defend only the timing rather than everything.
3. B is more useful. The costs are wrong is a judgement that invites contradiction. May be last year's figures is a checkable claim with a reason attached — the supplier raised prices in March — so it can be resolved by looking rather than by arguing.
4. It leaves the decision open and invites a reply. A ends with we should wait until spring, which is a verdict; B asks whether a spring start would be workable, which keeps the exchange going and makes agreement easier to reach.
5. The extra length is entirely framing: a concession, an explicit narrowing of the target, opinion frames, hedges on the judgements, a reason attached to the factual correction, and a question instead of a conclusion. None of it adds content and all of it changes how the content lands.
writing.successCriteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 3 explains checkability rather than politeness; answer 4 contrasts a verdict with an invitation; answer 5 identifies that the extra length is framing rather than content
writing.support: Underline the three objections in each version first. They occupy about a third of B and almost all of A, and that ratio is the answer to question 5.
writing.extension: Rewrite B to be as short as A while keeping the concession and the question. What did you have to sacrifice?

2. She did not reply. (Pattern 1 — ignored adds an intention you cannot see)

activities.title: Practice 5 — Rewrite something you sent
activities.instructionsAndItems:

activities.title: Practice 6 — Listen for the concession
activities.instructionsAndItems:

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Concede something first, then disagree — The concession tells the other person you understood them, so the disagreement reads as being about the substance rather than about not having listened.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: The case for doing it is strong — my reservation is the timing. — It names something specific that is being conceded and then names exactly what is under attack. A concession that names nothing reads as throat-clearing.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Yes — it is a full disagreement in the normal register — Anybody hearing it knows you disagree. English disagreement is usually indirect, and the indirectness is expected rather than evasive.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Because the hedging words that carry tone are the easiest to leave out — It is a mechanical result of a working vocabulary rather than a reflection of what the speaker thinks, and it is fixable with about six words.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Framing — concession, narrowing, hedges and a question — None of it adds content and all of it changes how the content lands, which is the sharpest demonstration in the unit that the difficulty is not grammar.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: It leaves the decision open and invites a reply — A ends with a verdict, which closes the exchange. B keeps it going, which makes agreement easier to reach without weakening the objection.
